source: Coulthart (2015) Improving the Analysis of Foreign Affairs: Evaluating Structured Analytic Techniques (PhD dissertation, Univ. of Pittsburgh)
finding: Repository abstract (full text was blocked by a bot check, so only the abstract was read). A systematic review of a sample of over 2,000 studies found moderate to strong support for ACH, brainstorming and devil's advocacy. Face-to-face collaboration reduced creativity. Weighing evidence mattered more than seeking disconfirming evidence. Conflict tended to improve analytic quality. A 21-student experiment backed the first two findings.
numbers: More than 2,000 sampled studies; survey of 80 analysts (1 in 3 never used SATs; training and perceived value predicted use, time pressure did not); experiment N=21 graduate intelligence students.
quote: evidence weighting mattered more than seeking disconfirming evidence
limits: Only the abstract was read. Per-technique counts and the quality grading are not visible here. The experiment is tiny (N=21). The dissertation is unpublished; its method is a 'modest attempt' per the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3 style design: weigh evidence by diagnosticity, do not just hunt for disconfirmation. Treat the 'moderate to strong' label as weak-to-medium evidence.

source: Martin (2025) The Relationship Between Structured Analytic Techniques and Intelligence Analysis Quality: Evidence from Content Analysis (PsyArXiv), describing Coulthart (2017) IJIC
finding: Martin's introduction summarizes Coulthart's published systematic review of the 12 CIA Tradecraft Primer techniques. Only 6 of the 12 had any empirical evaluation: Devil's Advocacy, ACH, Brainstorming, Alternative Futures Analysis, Red Teaming, Team A/Team B. The share of supporting studies ranged from 0 to 100 percent. Only the first three had evidence credibility above 'low'.
numbers: 6 of 12 techniques evaluated at all; support rate 0-100% per technique; 3 techniques above 'low' credibility. Also cited: survey of 80 analysts, 21% use SATs more than rarely; RAND review found 22 of 63 reports (~35%) used SATs.
quote: only the first three techniques listed above were found to have evidence credibility higher than 'low'
limits: Secondhand description of Coulthart (2017); the original paper (Taylor and Francis) was not opened. Credibility grading is Coulthart's own.
agent_relevance: Half of the standard SAT toolkit has no test at all. Do not copy a technique into the schema on authority alone; each operator needs our own measurement.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique: Lessons for the intelligence community (Intelligence and National Security, forthcoming)
finding: Review of every experiment that pits ACH against a no-SAT control. ACH as a whole shows little to no benefit on judgment quality and may harm it. Some parts (the matrix, hypothesis generation) may help. The authors advise against mandating ACH.
numbers: Google Scholar search returned 244 entries; 7 entries describing 6 distinct experiments met the criteria. Sample sizes: 12 (Lehner 2008), 50 analysts (Mandel 2018), 147 (Karvetski 2020), 227 (Karvetski and Mandel 2020), 39 (Whitesmith 2020), 191 (Maegherman 2021).
quote: ACH appears to offer little benefit to judgment and reasoning quality and it may even have detrimental effects
limits: Narrative review, not a pooled effect size (outcomes too different). Tasks are mostly lab scenarios with novices. Search used one engine. Authors also wrote two of the included studies.
agent_relevance: Strongest single counter to the Coulthart 'ACH is supported' headline. Argues against building ACH-style scoring as a core operator without a test.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) Table 3, tally of ACH effects across the six experiments
finding: Vote count by outcome. Confirmation bias reduction: one positive study (Lehner, non-analysts only), three null (Lehner analysts, Whitesmith, Maegherman). Accuracy of probabilities: null in 3 studies. Diagnosticity judgment: positive in Mandel/Dhami, harmful in Karvetski 2020 and Karvetski and Mandel 2020. Reliability of ratings given identical evidence: harmful. Use of base rates: harmful (Dhami 2019).
numbers: Confirmation bias: +1 / 0 / 3 null. Accuracy: 0 positive / 3 null (studies 2, 4, 5). Diagnosticity: 1 positive (2 reports of the same data) / 2 detrimental. Reliability and base-rate use: detrimental in one study each.
limits: Vote counting ignores study size and quality. Reading of table cells from a text extraction; small positional ambiguity.
agent_relevance: No outcome shows a replicated benefit. Confirmation-bias gains appear only where there is no domain expertise, which resembles a model with no prior; test that on our agent before assuming it.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? (Judgment and Decision Making), as summarized in Wilcox and Mandel 2023 Table 2
finding: Randomized trial with 50 UK intelligence analysts. ACH-trained analysts judged cue diagnosticity better than control (large effect). But they did not beat control on accuracy and were worse on coherence violations. Statistical fixes did far better: recalibration plus coherence-weighted aggregation removed 61 percent of judgment error.
numbers: N=50 analysts, ACH vs control, 4 hypotheses; accuracy = mean absolute error vs Bayesian answer; statistical post-processing eliminated 61% of error.
limits: Read through the Wilcox and Mandel table, not the original paper. One task, one organisation.
agent_relevance: Code-side recalibration and aggregation beat a thinking technique. Fits the schema rule that the program, not the model, does counting and combining.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help? (PsyArXiv)
finding: Largest ACH-vs-control test with uncertain evidence. ACH gave no advantage on any coherence test. Both groups were subadditive, unreliable and too conservative. The ACH group showed pseudo-diagnostic weighting (treating non-diagnostic evidence as diagnostic) and was slightly less reliable.
numbers: N=227, two hypotheses, six cases. Unreliability (mean absolute difference on identical evidence): ACH .22 [.19,.24] vs control .18 [.16,.20], d=0.20, p=.051. Another contrast: t(218)=1.14, p=.25, d=0.15 (no difference).
quote: The findings do not support the claim that ACH is effective at improving probabilistic judgment.
limits: Online Qualtrics panel of lay people; 1-slide ACH introduction, no training; task was gang graffiti attribution; unreliability effect borderline.
agent_relevance: A matrix of evidence against hypotheses can raise pseudo-diagnosticity. If we score evidence per hypothesis, use likelihood ratios and check for evidence that fits all hypotheses equally.

source: Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin (2020) Improving Probability Judgment in Intelligence Analysis: From Structured Analysis to Statistical Aggregation (Risk Analysis; preprint read)
finding: ACH was pitted against a factorized Bayes method. Neither improved accuracy or handled correlated evidence. ACH reduced coherence. Post-analytic statistical methods (coherentization and aggregation) gave large accuracy gains; averaged gain was just over one standard deviation of error.
numbers: N=147 Canadian adults (mushroom edibility task); 2x3 design (method x cue salience); aggregation improvement 'just over 1 SD reduction in error'; double-counting of perfectly correlated cues rose when the correlation was made salient.
quote: ACH in fact decreased the coherence of probability judgments
limits: Lay participants, no training in the preprint's ACH condition; one task type. Accuracy gain partly just variance reduction by averaging.
agent_relevance: Averaging many samples gains from variance reduction, which matches our G4 warning that samples from one model are not independent. Gains are bounded.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva and Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Study 1: the ACH-style matrix (hypotheses in columns) did not reduce confirmation bias. A matrix with hypotheses in rows did. Study 2: most Dutch military analysts did not show confirmation bias, so the bias premise behind ACH is doubtful for experts.
numbers: Study 1 N=161: chose the confirming hypothesis HypRow 39.2% (20), HypCol 61.8% (34), HypText 67.3% (37); chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009, phi=.24. Study 2 N=62 analysts: 19.4% confirmation strategy, 14.5% inconsistent, 66.1% balanced; 83.3% sensitive to evidence credibility; 91.9% non-additive.
quote: the majority of 62 Dutch military analysts did not suffer from confirmation bias
limits: Tests a feature of ACH, not ACH as a procedure. Study 1 used mostly female students. Study 2 analysts had no control group.
agent_relevance: Layout changes behaviour more than a procedure does. How we present hypotheses and evidence to the model may matter more than telling it to disconfirm. Cross-link subfield 05 (layout and presentation).

source: Dhami, Mandel and colleagues (2019) ACH in-task protocol study, summarized in Dhami et al. 2024 and Wilcox and Mandel 2023
finding: Same 50-analyst trial as b05, looking at what analysts actually did. 80 percent of the control group built an ACH-style matrix unprompted. Most ACH-trained analysts broke ACH rules, mainly by using confirming evidence. Only a small minority summed only consistent evidence. ACH analysts were less internally consistent and not more accurate.
numbers: N=50 analysts; 4 hypotheses, 12 evidence items; 80% of controls reformatted into a matrix.
limits: Secondhand through two later papers. Single organisation.
agent_relevance: Procedure compliance is low even for trained humans. A code-enforced step order (our schema) avoids this failure, but it does not show the steps themselves help.

source: Maegherman, Ask, Horselenberg and van Koppen (2021) Test of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses in legal decision-making (Applied Cognitive Psychology), via Dhami 2024 and Wilcox and Mandel 2023
finding: Randomized trial with law students. ACH group and control (who got a bias warning) both chose more disconfirming than confirming questions and rated exonerating evidence as more important. No group difference in guilt ratings. Only about a third of the ACH group used the matrix.
numbers: N=191; 38% of ACH participants complied and reported using the matrix; matrix helpfulness rated 57/100.
limits: Students; a short explanation of ACH only; legal not intelligence setting. Read via secondary summaries.
agent_relevance: A plain warning about bias did as well as ACH. A one-line instruction may buy what a multi-step technique buys, which is cheap to test on a model.

source: Whitesmith (2020) ACH experiment on confirmation bias and serial position, via Wilcox and Mandel 2023 Table 2
finding: With two hours of ACH training, ACH showed no significant reduction in confirmation bias or order effects. Confirmation bias also distorted how people used the ACH scoring.
numbers: N=39 (32 King's College London staff and students, 7 UK intelligence community); 8 participants (21%) showed confirmation bias.
limits: Small, underpowered; 2x2 design; the five-criterion bias definition leaves it unclear how many criteria count.
agent_relevance: Even a structured scoring step is open to the bias it is meant to cure. Same risk as an LLM scoring its own evidence.

source: Otzipka and Volbert (2026) The analysis of competing hypotheses and expert witness testimony: Counteracting adversarial allegiance in witness credibility assessments? (PLoS One)
finding: Preregistered online experiment, 2x3. ACH did not reduce allegiance bias, no interaction with the party that hired the expert. All groups weighted critical evidence more. Authors suggest ACH may act as a framework that lets biased assessment through because it has no rule for weighing evidence.
numbers: N=159 after exclusions (ACH 86, control 73). Credibility ratings: method F(1,153)=.21, p=.649; interaction F(2,153)=1.12, p=.328. Evidence score: method F(1,153)=1.79, p=.183.
quote: ACH method may act as a framework that facilitates biased assessment
limits: Online; many exclusions (78 failed knowledge checks); no formal ACH training; underpowered after dropping from 206 planned to 158.
agent_relevance: Newest null result. Notes the same list of prior nulls (Lehner, Whitesmith, Maegherman, Arbiyah 2023, Sauerland 2020). Matches the 'weigh evidence' finding in b01: structure without a weighing rule does not help.

source: Lehner, Adelman, Cheikes and Brown (2008) Confirmation bias in complex analyses (IEEE Trans. SMC-A), via RAND RR1408 and Wilcox and Mandel 2023
finding: Mitre experiment on the USS Iowa explosion case. ACH reduced confirmation bias only among participants with no intelligence background; no reduction for experienced analysts. Measured on individuals, not groups.
numbers: R&D corporation staff; 5 experienced analysts in ACH condition vs 7 in non-SAT condition; four evidence rounds; ACH tutorial modelled on Folker.
limits: Tiny sample. Wilcox and Mandel call it too underpowered for any conclusion on either effects or non-effects by experience.
agent_relevance: The oldest 'positive' ACH result is weak and applies to novices. The 'expert vs novice' split is the key boundary condition.

source: Artner, Girven, Bruce et al. (2016) Assessing the Value of Structured Analytic Techniques in the U.S. Intelligence Community (RAND RR-1408)
finding: RAND found SATs have little formal evaluation. Cited studies are dated, mixed and not IC-like: Folker 2000 (JMIC) found structured hypothesis testing markedly improved accuracy in one of two controlled experiments and had little effect in the other; Mitre 2004 found ACH cut confirmation bias only in non-professionals; Tetlock 2005 found scenario development reduced forecast accuracy in two experiments; devil's advocacy may raise confidence in the preferred hypothesis.
numbers: Folker: 2 experiments, 1 strong effect, 1 weak. Tetlock: 2 experiments, both show lower accuracy with scenarios.
quote: The few relevant studies are dated, produced mixed results, and did not fully replicate conditions in the IC
limits: Policy brief. Heuer and Pherson dispute the scenario result because the IC uses scenarios to outline futures, not to predict.
agent_relevance: Scenario or alternative-futures steps can hurt point-forecast accuracy. Use them for coverage and planning, not as a forecasting step.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Argues SATs spread without tests, driven by endorsement. Heuer never subjected ACH to experiments. ACH-trained analysts were more susceptible to unpacking effects than untrained peers. Judgment correctives can add noise. Calls for tournaments and rigorous trials, including post-analytic recalibration and aggregation.
numbers: No new sample sizes. Cites Kent's anecdote of 'serious possibility' read as odds from 1:4 to 4:1.
limits: Position paper by authors who also ran the ACH trials. Not an independent verdict.
agent_relevance: Gives the rule we want: any scaffold step is guilty until measured, and a step that adds judged noise can lose to plain sampling plus code aggregation.

source: Marcoci, Burgman, Kruger et al. (2019) Better Together: Reliable application of the post-9/11 and post-Iraq US intelligence tradecraft standards requires collective analysis (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Tradecraft-standards scoring (ICD 203) is unreliable for a single rater and needs groups. Raters disagree, and two of eight criteria add little.
numbers: 15 raters, 64 reports. Single-rater ICC 0.366 (95% CI 0.268-0.495); 2 raters 0.498; 3 raters 0.608; 15 raters 0.897. Mean Cronbach alpha 0.606; dropping criterion 8 lifts 3-rater ICC to 0.759.
limits: Novice raters, hypothetical reports; reliability not validity.
agent_relevance: Warns against LLM-as-judge for 'quality of reasoning' with a single call. If a judge step is needed, use several independent rating passes and check agreement.

source: Martin (2025) Content analysis of SWARM reports, tradecraft quality and accuracy (PsyArXiv)
finding: Across 138 reports from two IARPA CREATE challenges, quality-of-reasoning scores and accuracy correlated weakly. Number of unique techniques in a report predicted quality-of-reasoning but not accuracy. ACH's link to accuracy was slightly negative; Bayes theorem and Bayes nets were more positive. No technique reliably predicted accuracy, likely from low power.
numbers: N=138 reports (80 with accuracy). QoR vs accuracy r(77)=.25, p=.028 (zero-order r(78)=.30). Technique count to QoR: F(1,134)=33.29, R2=.19, r(135)=.46; to accuracy: F(1,77)=2.14, p=.15, r(78)=.23. ACH vs accuracy r=-.08. Top accuracy predictor Timeline r=.28.
quote: SATs have small positive correlations with IC norm adherence that compound
limits: Observational, not randomized. Teams chose their own techniques. Sample for accuracy needs N~126 per author power check.
agent_relevance: More technique use makes a report look more rigorous without making it more correct. Our scorer must use ground truth, not rubric adherence.

source: Korb, Nyberg, Oshni Alvandi et al. (2020) Individuals vs. BARD: Experimental evaluation of an online system for structured, collaborative Bayesian reasoning (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Positive counterexample: a structured method that builds Bayesian networks and uses Delphi-style group exchange beat unaided individuals by very large margins on three probabilistic reasoning problems over 5 weeks. The same team earlier found Glass delta 0.8 for BN building and 0.5-1.3 for Delphi interaction.
numbers: N=256: 25 teams of 6-9 using BARD vs 58 individuals with Google Suite. Glass delta 1.4-2.2 per problem.
limits: Problems designed by the same team and suited to Bayes nets; novice participants; effect smaller than in the earlier experiment (implementation differences).
agent_relevance: Structure helps when it forces explicit probability arithmetic on a problem that has a right answer. Supports code-run Bayesian updates over free-form critique.

source: Mandel (2015) Instruction in information structuring improves Bayesian judgment in intelligence analysts (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Brief instruction in natural-frequency trees improved the coherence of analysts' probability judgments and binary choices. Over four-fifths answered all eight problems additively after instruction, and over half already did before.
numbers: 43 intelligence analysts, before-after design on 8 Bayesian problems.
limits: Within-subject without a control group in the abstract; judged coherence, not accuracy of real forecasts; immediate post-test.
agent_relevance: The training that works is arithmetic structure (frequency format), not hypothesis rhetoric. Use counts and frequencies in prompts when asking for probabilities.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum and Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate (arXiv 2305.14325)
finding: LLM analogue of devil's advocacy and conflict. Debate among 3 agents for 2 rounds beat a single agent, plain majority vote, and self-reflection on arithmetic, grade-school math, chess, biographies and MMLU. Gains rose with agents and rounds up to about 4 rounds.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0 / 75.0 / 81.0 / 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4 / 102.1 / 102.2 / 122.9. Biographies 66.0 vs 73.8; MMLU 63.9 vs 71.1 (distinct personas 74.2); chess validity 29.3 vs 45.2. Rounds above 4 gave similar results.
limits: ChatGPT-class models (2023); small test sets (100 problems for arithmetic); majority baseline used same sampling. Later work (b21, b22, b23) finds weaker gains.
agent_relevance: The best case for conflict improving quality in LLMs. Our G4 says samples from one model are not independent, so test debate against equal-cost self-consistency before adopting.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett and Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs (ICML; arXiv 2311.17371)
finding: Benchmark of debate against single agent, self-consistency, ensemble refinement and Medprompt. Debate systems do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling. Multi-Persona was about 7 percent worse than Medprompt. Debate is sensitive to hyperparameters; tuning the agreement level lets some debates beat the rest.
numbers: Best accuracy (GPT-3.5 setting): MedQA Medprompt .65, Society of Mind .64, Self-Consistency .60, Single Agent .60, Multi-Persona .58. PubMedQA Medprompt .77, Single .75, Multi-Persona .70. MMLU self-consistency .78 vs Multi-Persona .72.
quote: multi-agent debating systems, in their current form, do not reliably outperform other proposed prompting strategies
limits: GPT-3.5 for most runs; multiple-choice benchmarks; accuracy differences are a few points on small sets.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the debate advantage when the baseline is equal-compute self-consistency. Do not pay for debate without that control.

source: Wang, Wang, Su, Tong and Song (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: Are multi-agent discussions the key? (ACL; arXiv 2402.18272)
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (one worked demonstration) reaches about the same accuracy as the best multi-agent discussion across tasks. Discussion helps only when the prompt has no demonstration.
quote: a single-agent LLM with strong prompts can achieve almost the same performance as the best existing discussion approach
limits: Small test sets; demonstrations carefully written for each task; GPT-3.5, Gemini Pro, Bard.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for the debate gain: it substitutes for missing task context. A good example in the prompt may beat the whole 'conflict' scaffold.

source: Wynn, Satija and Hadfield (2025) Talk isn't always cheap: Understanding failure modes in multi-agent debate (arXiv 2509.05396)
finding: Debate can lower accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Models flip from correct to incorrect to agree with peers. The flip rate is highest when the agent is alone in its answer and falls as more peers agree. Points to sycophancy and conformity, not reasoning.
numbers: MMLU, CommonSenseQA, GSM8K; 100 random samples per task, 5 seeds; accuracy fell with rounds in many mixed-capability groups, most strongly on MMLU and CommonSenseQA.
quote: models frequently shift from correct to incorrect answers in response to peer reasoning, favoring agreement over challenging flawed reasoning
limits: Particular model mixes; short debates; exact drop per configuration is in figures, not read here.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition on conflict. Debate needs a mechanism that rewards holding a correct answer. Links to G4 and the conformity subfield.

source: Liang, He, Jiao et al. (2023/2024) Encouraging divergent thinking in large language models through multi-agent debate (arXiv 2305.19118)
finding: Names the 'degeneration-of-thought' problem: once a model is confident, self-reflection stops producing new ideas. Proposes 'tit for tat' debate with a judge, claiming gains on commonsense machine translation and counter-intuitive arithmetic. Says modest disagreement works best and adaptive stopping and a judge are needed.
numbers: Abstract and introduction only were read in this session; task numbers were not extracted.
limits: Only the first page was readable; no numbers recorded. Smit 2024 later found Multi-Persona (this method) about 7% below Medprompt and 0.72 vs 0.78 for self-consistency on MMLU.
agent_relevance: Source of the claim that forced disagreement helps. Compare with G1: doubt only on a signal, not by default.

source: Sharma, Tong, Korbak et al. (2023/2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (ICLR; arXiv 2310.13548)
finding: Five assistants often give in under challenge. When asked 'Are you sure?' they apologize and flip even when right. A user hint of an incorrect answer cuts accuracy. Human preference data and preference models sometimes reward agreement over truth.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of questions after 'Are you sure?'; GPT-4 admits on 42%. A user suggesting an incorrect answer can cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2).
quote: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions
limits: Older models (2023); some numbers are read from text, not tables; newer models tuned against this.
agent_relevance: Direct risk to a devil's-advocate step: a model told to criticise its own correct answer will often cave. Supports G2: revise only from real failing output.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley and He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (Findings of EMNLP; arXiv 2403.00811, BiasBuster)
finding: Tests human-style biases (anchoring, framing, status quo, group attribution, primacy) in LLMs on admissions decisions. GPT-4 showed strong framing bias. Debiasing by awareness prompt gave small gains, few-shot debiasing sometimes broke the model, and letting the model rewrite its own prompt ('self-help') worked best, mainly for high-capacity models.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing; Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Self-help cut biased prompt elements to 0% (group attribution) and 2.7% (framing) for GPT-4; Llama models changed 40-52% of decisions in the anchoring self-help setup. Few-shot sometimes drove admission rates to 0 or 1.
limits: Synthetic admissions task; bias defined by pattern, not correctness; no accuracy outcome.
agent_relevance: Bias warnings help little; asking a strong model to clean its own prompt helps more. Few-shot debiasing can fail outright, so any debiasing step needs a check.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing multi-agent collaborative decision-making via ACH-inspired structured reasoning (arXiv 2508.11995)
finding: Only LLM paper found that builds directly on ACH. The decider agent evaluates answers under an ACH-style protocol and is trained in two stages (scaffolded, then scaffold removed). Beats voting and dictatorial deciders on MMLU, MMLU-Pro and ARC-Challenge. Keeping the scaffold alone hurt.
numbers: All-average accuracy: single agent 66.0; best voting 80.6; Homogeneous ACH-protocol 82.9; Qwen-7B-R1 87.6; AgentCDM 88.4. MMLU-Pro: single 47.4; AgentCDM 65.2 vs Qwen-7B-R1 58.0. Ablation (MMLU/MMLU-Pro/ARC): Full 78.5/65.2/96.0; vanilla prompt 72.6/52.5/89.0; scaffolding-only 68.1/49.4/84.0; exploration-only 71.5/52.1/89.7.
quote: rigid adherence to the structured protocol impairs generalization
limits: Small 7B models with training; compares against weak voting baselines; the structured protocol is 'ACH-inspired', not ACH. No equal-cost self-consistency baseline reported in the part read.
agent_relevance: The scaffold alone made things worse than a plain prompt; the gain came from training that absorbed the scaffold. For a no-training agent, expect rigid ACH steps to hurt. Matches Wilcox and Mandel's human finding.

source: Roberts (2025) LLM SATs FTW (SANS Emerging Threats Summit talk and blog), as summarized in the sats4llms wiki
finding: Practitioner build of GPT-4 tools for starbursting, ACH and key assumptions check. ACH works only as separate sequential calls (hypotheses, evidence for and against, then scores from -5 to +5). Single-prompt ACH fails. Chunking breaks the assumptions check across document parts. The human reviews and sets the final call.
numbers: One test: a key assumptions check on a 2025 report produced 30 assumptions 'of varying quality'. No accuracy measure.
limits: Anecdote, not an experiment. Read through a wiki summary of the blog, not the blog itself. No control condition.
agent_relevance: Tells us how to implement a SAT in code (separate calls, structured output) but gives no evidence that it improves answers.

source: sats4llms wiki (2026) SATs for LLM agents: hypotheses H1-H7 and evidence synthesis
finding: A wiki that maps SATs to LLM failures (ACH vs confirmation bias, devil's advocacy vs sycophancy, key assumptions check vs anchoring). It lists seven hypotheses and says explicitly they are untested; it holds no numeric LLM results. It records that the human evidence is mixed.
numbers: 12 sources ingested; 0 numerical results on SATs with LLMs.
limits: Secondary, mostly synthesis and speculation. Useful for the research agenda, not as evidence.
agent_relevance: Confirms the gap: as of mid-2026 we found no controlled test of classic SATs (ACH, devil's advocacy, red team) on LLM accuracy against an equal-cost baseline. This is a result our own bench could supply.

source: Search note (this session): LLM and AI studies on SAT effectiveness 2020-2026
finding: An arXiv title/abstract search for 'analysis of competing hypotheses' returned 4 papers: AgentCDM (2025, b27), a threat-actor LLM paper (Evron, 2026), a Havana syndrome essay (2024) and a fraud code-word paper (2021). A search for 'structured analytic techniques' with 'language model' returned none. Semantic Scholar and the arXiv API were rate-limited, and OpenAlex had no free budget, so coverage is partial.
numbers: 4 arXiv hits for ACH; 0 for SATs plus language model.
limits: One search engine; the Evron 2026 paper (arXiv 2610.35624) was not opened and is not scored here.
agent_relevance: The LLM-and-SAT literature is thin. Most LLM evidence on 'conflict' comes from the multi-agent debate line (b20-b24), not from intelligence-analysis tests.
